title: Can Large Language Models Understand Intermediate Representations in Compilers?
extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether large language models (LLMs) can understand compiler intermediate representations (IRs), rather than addressing any educational intervention or literacy outcome. The authors study a core technical question: how well current LLMs can reason over LLVM IR code across four tasks—control flow graph (CFG) reconstruction, IR decompilation into C++, code summarization, and execution reasoning. The motivation is that IRs are central to compilers and program analysis, but their low-level, instruction-oriented structure may pose challenges for models trained largely on natural language and high-level source code.

The approach is an empirical benchmark study comparing six state-of-the-art LLMs: GPT-4, GPT-3, DeepSeek R1, Gemma 2, Llama 3.1, and Code Llama. The evaluation uses a dataset derived from the HumanEval benchmark, consisting of 164 C++ programs compiled into LLVM IR at four optimization levels (-O0 to -O3). The authors design task-specific prompts and assess model outputs using quantitative metrics tailored to each task, such as CFG node/edge accuracy, decompilation completion and execution success, BLEU/ROUGE-L/METEOR for summarization, and assertion pass rates for execution reasoning.

There is no human participant population in this study; the context is automated evaluation of LLM performance on compiler-related code analysis tasks. The experiments appear to be computational and benchmark-based rather than classroom, school, or learner-facing. The paper is therefore not directly relevant to K-12 literacy or generative AI in education, though it may be relevant to AI capability assessment in software engineering.

The main conclusion is that current LLMs can parse some IR syntax and recover limited structural information, but they struggle with precise control flow reasoning, loop handling, instruction-level semantics, and faithful execution simulation. The authors find that models often rely on heuristic approximations rather than exact instruction-by-instruction reasoning, leading to errors in CFG reconstruction, decompilation, summarization, and execution tasks. They argue that improving IR understanding will likely require IR-specific fine-tuning, structured datasets, and architectures more sensitive to control flow and execution semantics.
quality_tier_rationale: This paper is an arXiv exploratory benchmark study in compiler/LLM reasoning, not K-12 education research. It is not peer-reviewed educational causal evidence and provides no school-based intervention, comparator, or learner outcome design relevant to the requested framework.
impact_tier_rationale: The study reports no K-12 literacy outcomes or education impacts. Its findings concern LLM performance on compiler intermediate representation tasks, so there is no demonstrated educational impact.
